Bourgeois 4
including his magisterial throwaway descriptions of houses, towns, scenes and places: of how
people looked, dressed, ate, drank, aspired and desired in a Hungary not so long ago, yet in a
way long ago.” 14  These portraits inspired Lukacs to use the novel ist’s descriptive techniques in
his own histor ies . He insisted that the novel and history were intertwined art forms, each giving
and taking style and content from the other.
In Historical Consciousness , Lukacs claimed that “In the broad sense, every novel is a
historical novel .” 15  This definition does not adhere to a set of arbitrarily chosen rules. For a novel
to be considered historical, it does not need to take place years before the author ’s life . It do es
not always recount the political and social events of a time , nor recreate the lives of certain
historical personages. Lukacs’s dictum is not an attempt to define the sub -genre. To Lukacs, a ny
novel that describe d rea l places, circumstances, and people could be considered historical . He
saw the novel as an intrinsically historical genre. Very early in his career, Lukacs went so far as
to predict the end of the novel and its absorption into histor ical writing .16  He saw in many
twentieth -century novelists an effort to write history with the form of a novel, rather than write a
novel with the help of history . The French J ea n Dutourd, American E.L. Doctorow, Russian
Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, and many more wrote novels for the primary purpose of preserving
history . More forebodingly , in his 1981 essay “Doctorow urlitzer or History in Ragtime ,” Lukacs
predict ed the end of serious literature in the West. Despite this later pessimism, Lukacs allowed
the novel to greatly influence his writing and teaching styles . His student John Rossi

Lukacs typically referred to novels from the nineteenth century, which he dubbed, “the
golden age of the novel ,” to show the historicity of the genre .18  He was not the first historian to
describe novels this way . Forty -six years before the publication of Lukacs’s Historical
Consciousness, the English historian Herbert Butterfield indicate the details a historian could
find in the novel . He even anticipated Lukacs’s recognition that “ The functions of historians and
novelists overlap; their dependence is mutual ; their approach is much the same – description, in
prose, always the description of some kind of past .” 19  In his essay The Historical Novel (1924) ,
Butterfield specifi ed what kind of material the novelist preserves :
though we may not seek to gather our historical facts from the novel, there are

This thesis began as an inquiry into José Ortega y Gasset’s Meditations on Quixote. I
intended to study Ortega’s view of the novel and how it influenced John Lukacs. As the project
evolved, the focus shifted to Lukacs. However, Ortega remained an instrumental figure to the
project insofar as he influenced Lukacs . However, Lukacs became the main study of the project
very early. The historiography of Luka cs ’s work is currently sparse. His students (John Rossi and
John Rodden) have written multiple articles about him. 88  Other Historians, such as Richard
Gamble, Lee Congdon, and John H. Ferrell have also written clearly about Lukacs’s legacy.

Some Hungarian writers wrote about him. Among others, t he historian and diplomat Géza
Jeszens ky, a friend of Lukacs, crafted an essay in memory of him. Many mention ed his love of
novels, but few went further. Lukacs’s reflections on the novel are intrinsically woven into many
of his other themes , such as the democratic age, historical consciousness, and others . For
some one to fully understand the novel’s significance , he must be acquainted with these themes.
In 2025, I worked with the John Lukacs papers at Notre Dame. Until 2019, no scholar
had access to these papers. Even now, only a small group has worked with them. Gamble is the
only historian who has both written about Lukacs and studied his archives. Letters to and from
novelists, lecture notes, and unpublished drafts added greatly to this project. It became even
clear er in the archives that Lukacs’s reflections on the novel went deeper permeated more than

John Lukacs (1924 -2019) is best remembered for his histories of modern Europe ,
America, and the Second World War , as well as his philosophy of history . After his death, a
variety of obituaries recounted his contributions on these topics. 1 Outside of obituaries, several
historians have explored his writing in bo th Hungarian and English .2 However, remembering him
as nothing more than a historian of modern civilization may obscure his lengthy meditations on
the novel. Lukacs the historian cannot be understood without his love of novels. Few have
studie d his extensive meditations on literature . Lee Congdon’s article “The Reactionary
Loyalties of John Lukacs” (2003) and Géza Jeszensky’s “Civis Hungaricus : For Our Mistakes,
Now We Alone Are Responsible ” (2023) mention Lukacs’s fascination but do little more. 3 The
Hungarian historian voraciously read novels, and this obsession shaped his view of the historical
craft. He most clearly articulated his indebtedness to the novel in his 1968 Historical

In Historical Consciousness , Lukacs claimed that “In the broad sense, every novel is a
historical novel .” 15  This definition does not adhere to a set of arbitrarily chosen rules. For a novel
to be considered historical, it does not need to take place years before the author ’s life . It do es
not always recount the political and social events of a time , nor recreate the lives of certain
historical personages. Lukacs’s dictum is not an attempt to define the sub -genre. To Lukacs, a ny
novel that describe d rea l places, circumstances, and people could be considered historical . He
saw the novel as an intrinsically historical genre. Very early in his career, Lukacs went so far as
to predict the end of the novel and its absorption into histor ical writing .16  He saw in many
twentieth -century novelists an effort to write history with the form of a novel, rather than write a
novel with the help of history . The French J ea n Dutourd, American E.L. Doctorow, Russian
Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, and many more wrote novels for the primary purpose of preserving
history . More forebodingly , in his 1981 essay “Doctorow urlitzer or History in Ragtime ,” Lukacs
predict ed the end of serious literature in the West. Despite this later pessimism, Lukacs allowed
the novel to greatly influence his writing and teaching styles . His student John Rossi

Bibliographical Essay
This thesis began as an inquiry into José Ortega y Gasset’s Meditations on Quixote. I
intended to study Ortega’s view of the novel and how it influenced John Lukacs. As the project
evolved, the focus shifted to Lukacs. However, Ortega remained an instrumental figure to the
project insofar as he influenced Lukacs . However, Lukacs became the main study of the project
very early. The historiography of Luka cs ’s work is currently sparse. His students (John Rossi and
John Rodden) have written multiple articles about him. 88  Other Historians, such as Richard
Gamble, Lee Congdon, and John H. Ferrell have also written clearly about Lukacs’s legacy.

# History.
Some Hungarian writers wrote about him. Among others, t he historian and diplomat Géza
Jeszens ky, a friend of Lukacs, crafted an essay in memory of him. Many mention ed his love of
novels, but few went further. Lukacs’s reflections on the novel are intrinsically woven into many
of his other themes , such as the democratic age, historical consciousness, and others . For
some one to fully understand the novel’s significance , he must be acquainted with these themes.
In 2025, I worked with the John Lukacs papers at Notre Dame. Until 2019, no scholar
had access to these papers. Even now, only a small group has worked with them. Gamble is the
only historian who has both written about Lukacs and studied his archives. Letters to and from
novelists, lecture notes, and unpublished drafts added greatly to this project. It became even
clear er in the archives that Lukacs’s reflections on the novel went deeper permeated more than
just his writing. Many materials have not been exp lored that may add to this discussion. For
example, later in life, Lukacs began and continued an extensive correspondence with the

American novelist Wendell Berry (1934 -present). These letters likely contain relevant
information to further studies on this topic. Lukacs also corresponded with the French historian
and novelist Jean Dutourd (1920 -2011), and the two developed a close frie ndship. 89  Other letters

# History.
about novelists like those to Cushing Strout and Truman Capote can be found in the archives as
well. Short discussions about the novel also surfaced in the George Kennan (1904 -2005)

John Lukacs (1924 -2019) is best remembered for his histories of modern Europe ,
America, and the Second World War , as well as his philosophy of history . After his death, a
variety of obituaries recounted his contributions on these topics. 1 Outside of obituaries, several
historians have explored his writing in bo th Hungarian and English .2 However, remembering him
as nothing more than a historian of modern civilization may obscure his lengthy meditations on
the novel. Lukacs the historian cannot be understood without his love of novels. Few have
studie d his extensive meditations on literature . Lee Congdon’s article “The Reactionary
Loyalties of John Lukacs” (2003) and Géza Jeszensky’s “Civis Hungaricus : For Our Mistakes,
Now We Alone Are Responsible ” (2023) mention Lukacs’s fascination but do little more. 3 The
Hungarian historian voraciously read novels, and this obsession shaped his view of the historical
craft. He most clearly articulated his indebtedness to the novel in his 1968 Historical

people looked, dressed, ate, drank, aspired and desired in a Hungary not so long ago, yet in a
way long ago.” 14  These portraits inspired Lukacs to use the novel ist’s descriptive techniques in
his own histor ies . He insisted that the novel and history were intertwined art forms, each giving

In Historical Consciousness , Lukacs claimed that “In the broad sense, every novel is a
historical novel .” 15  This definition does not adhere to a set of arbitrarily chosen rules. For a novel
to be considered historical, it does not need to take place years before the author ’s life . It do es
not always recount the political and social events of a time , nor recreate the lives of certain
historical personages. Lukacs’s dictum is not an attempt to define the sub -genre. To Lukacs, a ny
novel that describe d rea l places, circumstances, and people could be considered historical . He
saw the novel as an intrinsically historical genre. Very early in his career, Lukacs went so far as
to predict the end of the novel and its absorption into histor ical writing .16  He saw in many
twentieth -century novelists an effort to write history with the form of a novel, rather than write a
novel with the help of history . The French J ea n Dutourd, American E.L. Doctorow, Russian
Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, and many more wrote novels for the primary purpose of preserving
history . More forebodingly , in his 1981 essay “Doctorow urlitzer or History in Ragtime ,” Lukacs
predict ed the end of serious literature in the West. Despite this later pessimism, Lukacs allowed
the novel to greatly influence his writing and teaching styles . His student John Rossi

place with a small garden where you can keep ducks and hens. 48
Even with its mythical elements, Krúdy’s nove l painted a historical portrait . Its horses, baths,
music, and playing children all add to the recreation of an older Hungary . In a similar way, the

# History.
magical realism of Isabel Allende, Jorge Luis Borges, or Gabriel Garc ía M árquez infused Latin
American realities with mythical elements. The se authors also described historical landscapes
and characters. Therefore, chivalric literature, magical realism, and fantasy, even if they are
“corrupted” realities , do preserve the past. But the historian cannot confuse the mythical and the
historical elemen ts. H e is not interested in the mythical or an alternate past, but his own past.
When Lukacs spoke of the historical novel, he understood that some nove ls were more
historical than others . He even recognized, as did Ortega, a trend in modern literary history that
marked an increasing historical preoccupation among novelists . Ortega placed the beginning of
history -focused literature in 1605, with the appearance of Miguel Cervantes’ s Don Quijote de la
Mancha . This book, which Ortega referred to as “the first novel in point of time and in merit,”
was one of the first to separate itself from myt h.49  Cervantes took mythological and romantic
> 48 Gyula Krúdy, The Adventures of Sindbad, 21.  
> 49 José Ortega y Gasset, Meditations on Quixote, 111 .
Bourgeois 15
elements and turned them into caricatures of reality . The senile don Hidalgo looked at his reality
through the lens of the chivalric myth . The inns were castles. The prostitutes were damsels. The
windmills were giants. But d espite Hidalgo’s fantasies, the world always returned to reality. The
mythical elements were only illusions spurred by his imagination. Ortega wrote that “Cervantes
declare[d] that he [was] writing his book against the books of chivalry.” 50  In a later essay entitled
“Notes on the Novel,” Ortega anticipated Lukacs’s emphasis on historical details . He wrote,
“Cervantes fills all our senses with the genuine presence of his personages. We listen to their true
conversations, we see their actual movements.” 51  Don Quixote provide d historically accurate
images from the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries . For Ortega, Don Quijote is “at least as
close to our innermost sensibility as are the builders of the contemporary novel – Balzac,

# History.
Dickens, Flaubert, or Dostoievski.” 52  He mean t th at these novelists paid special attention to the
historical accuracy of their fictional settings. The ir novels preserve d images of the past.
Lukacs understood that fantastical literature did not excel at the production of historical
evidence . B ut even novelists who intentionally write historical novels do not always plausibly
recreate the past . For example, though Lukacs saw a n attempt at a histor y-infused novel in E.L.
Doctorow’s Ragtime (1975) , he also observed dangers that may mislead a careless historian.
Like many other novelists, Doctorow presented historical people such as Houdini, Freud, and
Emma Goldman as living, breathing characters in his novel. In doing so, he attributed actions
and patterns of thinking to historical person s that may not have correspond ed to the real person .
“[Doctorow] performs neat tricks,” wrote Lukacs, “making [real people] do things and say things

> 51 José Ortega y Gasset, “The Decline of the Novel,” in The Dehumanization of Art and Other Essays ,  
> trans. Helene Weyl (Princeton, NJ: Princeton University Press, 1968), 62 .  
> 52 José Ortega y Gasset, Meditations on Quixote, 111.
Bourgeois 16
they had not said ‘in fact’ but which will make them more ‘real.’ But it doesn’t.” 53  Doctorow
took real people and turned them into fictional characters . But he present ed them as historically
accurate re creations . In the attempt to make his novel feel real, Doctorow only attributed
historical names to fictional characters. In contrast, Balzac created fictional characters and
enlivened them with historical tendencies. The reader is aware that Balzac’s characters did not
exist. Doctorow presented his fictional Houdini as an equivalent to the historical person . As a
result, one may mista ke th e actions and words of the fiction for th e real . The result of this
fictional reimagining “is the confusion of what is imaginary with what is real, instead of a proper

# History.
understanding of [th e actors’] correspondence, of their complementarity: imaginary matters are
introduced, illegitimately, into past realities in the ‘name’ of history.” 54  Lukacs did not condemn
the novelist’s use of historical figures. But he did caution his readers against misinformation .
Because of this confusion of fiction and real ity , the reader should regard historical fictio n with
skepticism . This skepticism is not n ew . The historian looks at all evidence with a discerning eye .
He carefully judges the validity of every historical fragment. He must do the same when faced
with fictional representations of real people. Lukacs contrasted this dangerous synthesis of
fiction and history with more reliable historical fiction . For example, Flaubert repre sented a type
of nineteenth -century French woman with Madame Bovary , and Balzac typified a French miser
with Felix Grandet. 55  These novelists avoid ed misattribution by creating their own characters.

> 289.  
> 54 John Lukacs, Historical Consciousness , 124 -5.  
> 55 Gustave Flaubert, Madame Bovary ,trans. Gerard Hopkins ( London: Avenel Books, 1986 );Honoré de  
> Balzac, Eugénie Grandet ,trans. Sylvia Raphael ( New York, NY :Oxford University Press, 2003). Bourgeois 17
Lukacs did more th an e xplain how the historian can use novels. He also used the
novelist’s techniques in his own work. An unfinished draft of a n introduction to a novel can be
found in his archives . His A Thread of Years (1998) presents a series of fictional vignettes that
capture life in the twentieth century . In a 2009 interview with Donald Yerxa, he claimed that, of
his thirty books , it was his favorite, “though admittedly a very strange book of mine that is
neither history nor literature. ”56  In it, he present ed “everyday people whose plausibility exists

# History.
only because of the historical reality of their places and times.” 57  Fictional vignettes acted as a
history of “the petite musique of a grande histoire, the decline of a civilization.” 58  The novel’ s
influence on Lukacs even surfaces in his more traditional histories. In his Budapest 1900: a
Historical Portrait of a City and Its Culture (1998) , Lukacs began by recreating the city’s
atmosphere on the day of a specific event in 1900 – the Hungarian artist Mih ály Munk ácsy’s
funeral. Lukacs prepared the reader to explore Budapest by forming the city in his mind. He
rebuilt the world using the novelist’s descriptive techniques . Lukacs, born too late t o attend
Munkacsy’s funeral, still recaptured th e city’s glamour at that time :
At Octagon Square, a mile down Andrássy Avenue, [where] a trumpeter halted
the march, to direct the procession to turn leftward to the Ring. The bishops and
the ministers stepped into their carriages. In front of the terraces of the
coffeehouses gypsy bands p layed Munkácsy’s favorite Hungarian songs. Stiff in
black stood the Carpenters’ and the Housepainters’ Guild, and the choral society
of a factory sent the bass of their threnody up the afternoon sky. There was a
moment of disturbance: the chorus of the Sch ool of Blind Children was told to
step forward to sing, but the mounted policeman in front had not been alerted, he
rode into their frightened ranks to push them back. But there was no other
commotion, save for the fear of some people that the narrow ornam ental balconies

Bourgeois 18
of the newly built monumental apartment houses might crumble under the weight
of the assembled spectators. 59

# History.
This passage would fit in the novels of Krúdy or Kos ztol ányi . Rather than begin with a slog of
historical data, Lukacs reproduced Budapest in 1900 . The first chapter gave the reader an instant
familiarity with the city . It prepared him to learn more about it . A more bitter example of his
novelistic descriptions comes from his 1945: Year Zero (1978) . At the end of the Second World
War, a fear -ridden Lukacs scoured the streets of a death -filled Budapest:
the cities and towns of Central Europe stank with their corpses. One day this
writer, thin as a rail and famished, was going up to the hills above his native city
with a beautiful woman, to lie on a green meadow spangled with wildflowers…
Wending his way t hrough the ruined streets, he bought a handful of apricots from
a peasant woman for a handful of paper money. He had to wend his way between
the enormous heaps of collapsed houses under some of which lay hundreds of
bodies freshly dead. Their smell swam in his nostrils, as did the scent of apricots
and the flowers. 60
Again, he relied on his descriptive skills to reimagine a decimated Europe. This image even
highlights the juxtaposition of the same place at a different time . Only 45 years after 1900,
Luka cs beheld rubble and corpses where the re used to be grand avenues and trumpeted marchers.
These novelesque descriptions of Budapest in 1900 and 1945 belong to the history of that city.
The y also represent a common technique in Lukacs’s work. In a letter from 1985, he synthesized
how the novelist and historian’s techniques blend together: “where the novelist’s craft and talent
comes in is in the quality of his imaginative prose – but he does not let his imagination run away

# History.
> 59 The rest of the passage reads, “On the second -story balcony of No. 44 Elizabeth Ring stood a small  
> white -bearded figure, the grand old man of Hungarian literature, Mór Jókai. He lifted his hat as the procession  
> passed under him. Women curtsied; there were women who knelt. A mile down the Ring, then another turn, on to

into uncharted realms of unknown and unknowable things.” 61  He did just that in his own writing.
He wrote with the limits of the historian and the imagination of the poet. What the historian
Robert H. Ferrell admired about Lukacs ’ The Duel (1992) , can be applied to many of his
histories, that “ Lukacs [took] a narrative that lesser writers drew in prose and turn[ed] it to
poetry, but the poet [did] not depart from the facts of the c ase.” 62  In his histories, Lukacs
demonstrated that his own histories benefited from t he novelist’s descriptive techniques .63
In 198 1, Lukacs reiterated his observation that many novelists were becoming more
interested in history . Th ey experimented with the past in new and more complex ways . In their
novels, the narrative became secondary to the histor ical details. Though admitting that his term
was imperfect, Lukacs called these “novelistic histories.” 64  He described this historical
prioritization as mov ing history from the background into the foreground. By history in the

# History.
background, Lukacs referred to “the classic historical novel [in which] the great events of history
are painted on a large canvas in order to lend depth to the story, to give an added dimension to
the main characters.” 65  Tolstoy’s War and Peace, which used the Napoleonic wars to move the
narrative along , fit s this description. Th e wars provided the backdrop for events of the novel.

Bibliographical Essay
This thesis began as an inquiry into José Ortega y Gasset’s Meditations on Quixote. I
intended to study Ortega’s view of the novel and how it influenced John Lukacs. As the project
evolved, the focus shifted to Lukacs. However, Ortega remained an instrumental figure to the
project insofar as he influenced Lukacs . However, Lukacs became the main study of the project
very early. The historiography of Luka cs ’s work is currently sparse. His students (John Rossi and
John Rodden) have written multiple articles about him. 88  Other Historians, such as Richard
Gamble, Lee Congdon, and John H. Ferrell have also written clearly about Lukacs’s legacy.

# History.
Some Hungarian writers wrote about him. Among others, t he historian and diplomat Géza
Jeszens ky, a friend of Lukacs, crafted an essay in memory of him. Many mention ed his love of
novels, but few went further. Lukacs’s reflections on the novel are intrinsically woven into many
of his other themes , such as the democratic age, historical consciousness, and others . For
some one to fully understand the novel’s significance , he must be acquainted with these themes.
In 2025, I worked with the John Lukacs papers at Notre Dame. Until 2019, no scholar
had access to these papers. Even now, only a small group has worked with them. Gamble is the
only historian who has both written about Lukacs and studied his archives. Letters to and from
novelists, lecture notes, and unpublished drafts added greatly to this project. It became even
clear er in the archives that Lukacs’s reflections on the novel went deeper permeated more than
just his writing. Many materials have not been exp lored that may add to this discussion. For
example, later in life, Lukacs began and continued an extensive correspondence with the

information to further studies on this topic. Lukacs also corresponded with the French historian
and novelist Jean Dutourd (1920 -2011), and the two developed a close frie ndship. 89  Other letters

# History.
about novelists like those to Cushing Strout and Truman Capote can be found in the archives as
well. Short discussions about the novel also surfaced in the George Kennan (1904 -2005)

These archives revealed how immersed Lukacs was within the world of literature. Novels
fundamentally formed the way he thought about history.
Hundreds of novels could be used to help demonstrate Lukacs’s points. I have tried to
limit this essay to novels that Lukacs himself read and used. The French novelists – Balzac,
Maupassant, Stendhal, Flaubert, Dutourd, and Proust – are the most consistently returned to in
Lukacs’s writing. Thus, they deserved special emphasis in this essay . Though not as represented,
Leo Tolstoy and Fyodor Dostoyevsky appear frequently in Lukacs’s work. He heavily criticized
them for a variety of reasons . This criticism al one c ould fill an entire essay . Perhaps the most

This omission is interesting, since he had Lukács as a professor in his undergraduate years . In

never mentioned it in his published works, the novel demonstrates many of his conclusions. All

John Lukacs (1924 -2019) is best remembered for his histories of modern Europe ,
America, and the Second World War , as well as his philosophy of history . After his death, a
variety of obituaries recounted his contributions on these topics. 1 Outside of obituaries, several
historians have explored his writing in bo th Hungarian and English .2 However, remembering him
as nothing more than a historian of modern civilization may obscure his lengthy meditations on
the novel. Lukacs the historian cannot be understood without his love of novels. Few have
studie d his extensive meditations on literature . Lee Congdon’s article “The Reactionary
Loyalties of John Lukacs” (2003) and Géza Jeszensky’s “Civis Hungaricus : For Our Mistakes,
Now We Alone Are Responsible ” (2023) mention Lukacs’s fascination but do little more. 3 The
Hungarian historian voraciously read novels, and this obsession shaped his view of the historical
craft. He most clearly articulated his indebtedness to the novel in his 1968 Historical

his own histor ies . He insisted that the novel and history were intertwined art forms, each giving
and taking style and content from the other.
In Historical Consciousness , Lukacs claimed that “In the broad sense, every novel is a
historical novel .” 15  This definition does not adhere to a set of arbitrarily chosen rules. For a novel
to be considered historical, it does not need to take place years before the author ’s life . It do es
not always recount the political and social events of a time , nor recreate the lives of certain
historical personages. Lukacs’s dictum is not an attempt to define the sub -genre. To Lukacs, a ny
novel that describe d rea l places, circumstances, and people could be considered historical . He
saw the novel as an intrinsically historical genre. Very early in his career, Lukacs went so far as
to predict the end of the novel and its absorption into histor ical writing .16  He saw in many
twentieth -century novelists an effort to write history with the form of a novel, rather than write a
novel with the help of history . The French J ea n Dutourd, American E.L. Doctorow, Russian
Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, and many more wrote novels for the primary purpose of preserving
history . More forebodingly , in his 1981 essay “Doctorow urlitzer or History in Ragtime ,” Lukacs
predict ed the end of serious literature in the West. Despite this later pessimism, Lukacs allowed
the novel to greatly influence his writing and teaching styles . His student John Rossi

Lukacs typically referred to novels from the nineteenth century, which he dubbed, “the
golden age of the novel ,” to show the historicity of the genre .18  He was not the first historian to
describe novels this way . Forty -six years before the publication of Lukacs’s Historical
Consciousness, the English historian Herbert Butterfield indicate the details a historian could
find in the novel . He even anticipated Lukacs’s recognition that “ The functions of historians and
novelists overlap; their dependence is mutual ; their approach is much the same – description, in
prose, always the description of some kind of past .” 19  In his essay The Historical Novel (1924) ,
Butterfield specifi ed what kind of material the novelist preserves :
though we may not seek to gather our historical facts from the novel, there are
more subtle things, unconscious prejudices and unformulated sentiments that we
take in unawares, there are pictures that haunt us, there is an atmosphere that
compels us, and i f we find nothing else we find the sentiment of history, the
feeling for the past, in the historical novel. On one side, therefore, the historical
novel is a “form” of history. It is a way of treating the past. 20
Butterfield’s distinction between facts and subtle sentiments deserves emphasis. Both he and
Lukacs understood that the historian did more than connect a sequence of events or record data.

Lukacs understood that fantastical literature did not excel at the production of historical

and patterns of thinking to historical person s that may not have correspond ed to the real person .

the cities and towns of Central Europe stank with their corpses. One day this
writer, thin as a rail and famished, was going up to the hills above his native city
with a beautiful woman, to lie on a green meadow spangled with wildflowers…
Wending his way t hrough the ruined streets, he bought a handful of apricots from
a peasant woman for a handful of paper money. He had to wend his way between
the enormous heaps of collapsed houses under some of which lay hundreds of
bodies freshly dead. Their smell swam in his nostrils, as did the scent of apricots
and the flowers. 60

Bibliographical Essay
This thesis began as an inquiry into José Ortega y Gasset’s Meditations on Quixote. I
intended to study Ortega’s view of the novel and how it influenced John Lukacs. As the project
evolved, the focus shifted to Lukacs. However, Ortega remained an instrumental figure to the
project insofar as he influenced Lukacs . However, Lukacs became the main study of the project
very early. The historiography of Luka cs ’s work is currently sparse. His students (John Rossi and
John Rodden) have written multiple articles about him. 88  Other Historians, such as Richard
Gamble, Lee Congdon, and John H. Ferrell have also written clearly about Lukacs’s legacy.

# History.
Some Hungarian writers wrote about him. Among others, t he historian and diplomat Géza
Jeszens ky, a friend of Lukacs, crafted an essay in memory of him. Many mention ed his love of
novels, but few went further. Lukacs’s reflections on the novel are intrinsically woven into many
of his other themes , such as the democratic age, historical consciousness, and others . For
some one to fully understand the novel’s significance , he must be acquainted with these themes.
In 2025, I worked with the John Lukacs papers at Notre Dame. Until 2019, no scholar
had access to these papers. Even now, only a small group has worked with them. Gamble is the
only historian who has both written about Lukacs and studied his archives. Letters to and from
novelists, lecture notes, and unpublished drafts added greatly to this project. It became even
clear er in the archives that Lukacs’s reflections on the novel went deeper permeated more than
just his writing. Many materials have not been exp lored that may add to this discussion. For

John Lukacs (1924 -2019) is best remembered for his histories of modern Europe ,
America, and the Second World War , as well as his philosophy of history . After his death, a
variety of obituaries recounted his contributions on these topics. 1 Outside of obituaries, several
historians have explored his writing in bo th Hungarian and English .2 However, remembering him
as nothing more than a historian of modern civilization may obscure his lengthy meditations on
the novel. Lukacs the historian cannot be understood without his love of novels. Few have
studie d his extensive meditations on literature . Lee Congdon’s article “The Reactionary
Loyalties of John Lukacs” (2003) and Géza Jeszensky’s “Civis Hungaricus : For Our Mistakes,
Now We Alone Are Responsible ” (2023) mention Lukacs’s fascination but do little more. 3 The
Hungarian historian voraciously read novels, and this obsession shaped his view of the historical
craft. He most clearly articulated his indebtedness to the novel in his 1968 Historical

especially interested in historical novels except in certain instances.” 6 His love of history fueled
his reading of novels , and he did not limit himself to the category of “the historical novel .” The
thing he “relished in certain novels was every kind of historical detail.” 7

admired F. Scott Fitzgerald as much as he did Charles Dickens. He read and reread the novels of
Anthony Trollope into old age. 8 He recalled that in his teenage years, he “discovered the delights

More than any other novelist, Gyula Krúdy molded the way Lukacs thought and wrote .
This Hungarian’s novels were one of Lukacs’ great loves, alongside cigars and brandy. Géza
Jeszensky recalled that “His style and language were shaped by Hungarian literature, above all

greatest, of all prose writers of the last one hundred years.” 12  Until his death in 1933 , this

including his magisterial throwaway descriptions of houses, towns, scenes and places: of how
people looked, dressed, ate, drank, aspired and desired in a Hungary not so long ago, yet in a
way long ago.” 14  These portraits inspired Lukacs to use the novel ist’s descriptive techniques in
his own histor ies . He insisted that the novel and history were intertwined art forms, each giving
and taking style and content from the other.
In Historical Consciousness , Lukacs claimed that “In the broad sense, every novel is a
historical novel .” 15  This definition does not adhere to a set of arbitrarily chosen rules. For a novel
to be considered historical, it does not need to take place years before the author ’s life . It do es
not always recount the political and social events of a time , nor recreate the lives of certain
historical personages. Lukacs’s dictum is not an attempt to define the sub -genre. To Lukacs, a ny
novel that describe d rea l places, circumstances, and people could be considered historical . He
saw the novel as an intrinsically historical genre. Very early in his career, Lukacs went so far as
to predict the end of the novel and its absorption into histor ical writing .16  He saw in many
twentieth -century novelists an effort to write history with the form of a novel, rather than write a
novel with the help of history . The French J ea n Dutourd, American E.L. Doctorow, Russian
Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, and many more wrote novels for the primary purpose of preserving
history . More forebodingly , in his 1981 essay “Doctorow urlitzer or History in Ragtime ,” Lukacs
predict ed the end of serious literature in the West. Despite this later pessimism, Lukacs allowed
the novel to greatly influence his writing and teaching styles . His student John Rossi

Lukacs typically referred to novels from the nineteenth century, which he dubbed, “the
golden age of the novel ,” to show the historicity of the genre .18  He was not the first historian to
describe novels this way . Forty -six years before the publication of Lukacs’s Historical
Consciousness, the English historian Herbert Butterfield indicate the details a historian could
find in the novel . He even anticipated Lukacs’s recognition that “ The functions of historians and
novelists overlap; their dependence is mutual ; their approach is much the same – description, in
prose, always the description of some kind of past .” 19  In his essay The Historical Novel (1924) ,
Butterfield specifi ed what kind of material the novelist preserves :
though we may not seek to gather our historical facts from the novel, there are
more subtle things, unconscious prejudices and unformulated sentiments that we
take in unawares, there are pictures that haunt us, there is an atmosphere that
compels us, and i f we find nothing else we find the sentiment of history, the
feeling for the past, in the historical novel. On one side, therefore, the historical
novel is a “form” of history. It is a way of treating the past. 20
Butterfield’s distinction between facts and subtle sentiments deserves emphasis. Both he and
Lukacs understood that the historian did more than connect a sequence of events or record data.

Bibliographical Essay
This thesis began as an inquiry into José Ortega y Gasset’s Meditations on Quixote. I
intended to study Ortega’s view of the novel and how it influenced John Lukacs. As the project
evolved, the focus shifted to Lukacs. However, Ortega remained an instrumental figure to the
project insofar as he influenced Lukacs . However, Lukacs became the main study of the project
very early. The historiography of Luka cs ’s work is currently sparse. His students (John Rossi and
John Rodden) have written multiple articles about him. 88  Other Historians, such as Richard
Gamble, Lee Congdon, and John H. Ferrell have also written clearly about Lukacs’s legacy.

# History.
Some Hungarian writers wrote about him. Among others, t he historian and diplomat Géza
Jeszens ky, a friend of Lukacs, crafted an essay in memory of him. Many mention ed his love of
novels, but few went further. Lukacs’s reflections on the novel are intrinsically woven into many
of his other themes , such as the democratic age, historical consciousness, and others . For
some one to fully understand the novel’s significance , he must be acquainted with these themes.
In 2025, I worked with the John Lukacs papers at Notre Dame. Until 2019, no scholar
had access to these papers. Even now, only a small group has worked with them. Gamble is the
only historian who has both written about Lukacs and studied his archives. Letters to and from
novelists, lecture notes, and unpublished drafts added greatly to this project. It became even
clear er in the archives that Lukacs’s reflections on the novel went deeper permeated more than
just his writing. Many materials have not been exp lored that may add to this discussion. For
example, later in life, Lukacs began and continued an extensive correspondence with the

# The Historical Society: April Issue of Historically Speaking on Project Muse
## Saturday, April 25, 2009
### April Issue of _Historically Speaking_ on Project Muse
The April issue of Historically Speaking is up on Project Muse. Access is available by individual purchase or through college and university libraries. This issue includes interviews with Donald Worster, David Hackett Fischer, and Laurel Thatcher Ulrich; a review essay; two assessments of civil rights history; and a variety of articles.
Historically Speaking, Volume 10, Number 2, April 2009
Table of Contents
Massacre in Munich: The Olympic Terror Attacks of 1972 in Historical Perspective
David Clay Large
We Have Seen the Enemy and It Is Not David McCullough
Edward Gray
The Importance of Studying Ordinary Lives: An Interview with Laurel Thatcher Ulrich
Conducted by Randall J. Stephens
Why Dryasdust? Historians in Fiction
Beverley Southgate
The Ends of the Earth and the “Heroic Age” of Polar Exploration: A Review Essay
Katrin Schultheiss
Champlain’s Dream: An Interview with David Hackett Fischer
Conducted by Donald A. Yerxa
Fighting Bad History with Good, or, Why Historians Must Get on the Web Now
Marshall Poe
Adieu to Lebanon
Fred S. Naiden and Kenneth W. Harl
JOHN MUIR'S PASSION
John Muir and the Religion of Nature
Donald Worster
John Muir’s Passion for Nature: An Interview with Donald Worster
Conducted by Donald A. Yerxa
CIVIL RIGHTS HISTORIOGRAPHY: TWO PERSPECTIVES
Reconsidering the “Long Civil Rights Movement”
Eric Arnesen
The Lost Decade of Civil Rights
David L. Chappell
Letters

John Lukacs and the Convergence of Literature and History
Ethan Bourgeois
Collegiate Scholars Thesis
March 13, 2026 Bourgeois 1
John Lukacs (1924 -2019) is best remembered for his histories of modern Europe ,
America, and the Second World War , as well as his philosophy of history . After his death, a
variety of obituaries recounted his contributions on these topics. 1 Outside of obituaries, several
historians have explored his writing in bo th Hungarian and English .2 However, remembering him
as nothing more than a historian of modern civilization may obscure his lengthy meditations on
the novel. Lukacs the historian cannot be understood without his love of novels. Few have
studie d his extensive meditations on literature . Lee Congdon’s article “The Reactionary
Loyalties of John Lukacs” (2003) and Géza Jeszensky’s “Civis Hungaricus : For Our Mistakes,
Now We Alone Are Responsible ” (2023) mention Lukacs’s fascination but do little more. 3 The
Hungarian historian voraciously read novels, and this obsession shaped his view of the historical
craft. He most clearly articulated his indebtedness to the novel in his 1968 Historical

of the two can train the historian to understand the past with the help of novels . For Lukacs, the
reading of novels was more than a pastime. Novels instrumentally formed the way he thought.
This obsession with novels began before he devoted his career to history. In his autobiography,
Confessions of an Original Sinner (1991) , he remembered, “Around the age of thirteen I became
an avid reader of novels – of all kinds of novels, not only historical ones; in fact, I was not
texts.6:
# History.
especially interested in historical novels except in certain instances.” 6 His love of history fueled
his reading of novels , and he did not limit himself to the category of “the historical novel .” The
thing he “relished in certain novels was every kind of historical detail.” 7
Lukacs found these details in a variety of novels from across Europe and America. He
admired F. Scott Fitzgerald as much as he did Charles Dickens. He read and reread the novels of
Anthony Trollope into old age. 8 He recalled that in his teenage years, he “discovered the delights

Maupassant, Gustave Flaubert, and Stendhal taught Lukacs to see history in literature . As early
as 1959, Lukacs illustrated to an audience at Bryn Mawr College how these French novelists
preserved people, circumstances, and atmospheres from history .10  In that same lectu re he
contrasted them with the Russian novelists Leo Tolstoy and Fyodor Dostoyevsky, whom he
criticized for their ideological emphases . While Lukacs believed that every novel is histor ical , he
also cautioned that some historical novels convey false realities . However, his focus remained on

More than any other novelist, Gyula Krúdy molded the way Lukacs thought and wrote .
This Hungarian’s novels were one of Lukacs’ great loves, alongside cigars and brandy. Géza
Jeszensky recalled that “His style and language were shaped by Hungarian literature, above all
by Gyula Krúdy and De zs ő Kosztolányi.” 11  To Lukacs, Kr údy was “the most magical, if not the
greatest, of all prose writers of the last one hundred years.” 12  Until his death in 1933 , this
“magician of the Magyar language” wrote prolifically .13  Yet, he is vir tually unknown outside
Hungary. I n Krúdy’s novels, Lukacs found “the rich fullness of historical details of every kind,

Bourgeois 4
including his magisterial throwaway descriptions of houses, towns, scenes and places: of how
people looked, dressed, ate, drank, aspired and desired in a Hungary not so long ago, yet in a
way long ago.” 14  These portraits inspired Lukacs to use the novel ist’s descriptive techniques in
his own histor ies . He insisted that the novel and history were intertwined art forms, each giving
and taking style and content from the other.
In Historical Consciousness , Lukacs claimed that “In the broad sense, every novel is a
historical novel .” 15  This definition does not adhere to a set of arbitrarily chosen rules. For a novel
to be considered historical, it does not need to take place years before the author ’s life . It do es
not always recount the political and social events of a time , nor recreate the lives of certain
historical personages. Lukacs’s dictum is not an attempt to define the sub -genre. To Lukacs, a ny
novel that describe d rea l places, circumstances, and people could be considered historical . He
saw the novel as an intrinsically historical genre. Very early in his career, Lukacs went so far as
to predict the end of the novel and its absorption into histor ical writing .16  He saw in many
twentieth -century novelists an effort to write history with the form of a novel, rather than write a
novel with the help of history . The French J ea n Dutourd, American E.L. Doctorow, Russian
Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, and many more wrote novels for the primary purpose of preserving
history . More forebodingly , in his 1981 essay “Doctorow urlitzer or History in Ragtime ,” Lukacs
predict ed the end of serious literature in the West. Despite this later pessimism, Lukacs allowed
the novel to greatly influence his writing and teaching styles . His student John Rossi

remembered that “In his classes John included on his reading lists works of fiction and relatively
few academic histories.” 17  He also used the descriptive skills of the novelist in his own histories .
Lukacs typically referred to novels from the nineteenth century, which he dubbed, “the
golden age of the novel ,” to show the historicity of the genre .18  He was not the first historian to
describe novels this way . Forty -six years before the publication of Lukacs’s Historical
Consciousness, the English historian Herbert Butterfield indicate the details a historian could
find in the novel . He even anticipated Lukacs’s recognition that “ The functions of historians and
novelists overlap; their dependence is mutual ; their approach is much the same – description, in
prose, always the description of some kind of past .” 19  In his essay The Historical Novel (1924) ,
Butterfield specifi ed what kind of material the novelist preserves :
though we may not seek to gather our historical facts from the novel, there are
more subtle things, unconscious prejudices and unformulated sentiments that we
take in unawares, there are pictures that haunt us, there is an atmosphere that
compels us, and i f we find nothing else we find the sentiment of history, the
feeling for the past, in the historical novel. On one side, therefore, the historical
novel is a “form” of history. It is a way of treating the past. 20
Butterfield’s distinction between facts and subtle sentiments deserves emphasis. Both he and
Lukacs understood that the historian did more than connect a sequence of events or record data.

Bibliographical Essay
This thesis began as an inquiry into José Ortega y Gasset’s Meditations on Quixote. I
intended to study Ortega’s view of the novel and how it influenced John Lukacs. As the project
evolved, the focus shifted to Lukacs. However, Ortega remained an instrumental figure to the
project insofar as he influenced Lukacs . However, Lukacs became the main study of the project
very early. The historiography of Luka cs ’s work is currently sparse. His students (John Rossi and
John Rodden) have written multiple articles about him. 88  Other Historians, such as Richard
Gamble, Lee Congdon, and John H. Ferrell have also written clearly about Lukacs’s legacy.
texts.42:
# History.
Some Hungarian writers wrote about him. Among others, t he historian and diplomat Géza
Jeszens ky, a friend of Lukacs, crafted an essay in memory of him. Many mention ed his love of
novels, but few went further. Lukacs’s reflections on the novel are intrinsically woven into many
of his other themes , such as the democratic age, historical consciousness, and others . For
some one to fully understand the novel’s significance , he must be acquainted with these themes.
In 2025, I worked with the John Lukacs papers at Notre Dame. Until 2019, no scholar
had access to these papers. Even now, only a small group has worked with them. Gamble is the
only historian who has both written about Lukacs and studied his archives. Letters to and from
novelists, lecture notes, and unpublished drafts added greatly to this project. It became even
clear er in the archives that Lukacs’s reflections on the novel went deeper permeated more than
just his writing. Many materials have not been exp lored that may add to this discussion. For
example, later in life, Lukacs began and continued an extensive correspondence with the

Lukacs the historian cannot be understood without his love of novels. Few have studie d his extensive meditations on literature . These refl ections help to explain many broader themes in Lukacs’s work while also giving insights into how to become a better historian. As Lukacs indicated in and beyond Historical Consciousness, novelists and historians have a great deal in common. His comparison of the two can train the historian to understand the past with the help of novels . For Lukacs, the reading of novels was more than a pastime. Novels instrumentally formed the way he thought. This obsession with novels began before he devoted his career to history. In his autobiography, Confessions of an Original Sinner (1991) , he remembered, “Around the age of thirteen I became an avid reader of novels – of all kinds of novels, not only historical ones; in fact, I was not # History. especially interested in historical novels except in certain instances.” 6 His love of history fueled his reading of novels , and he did not limit himself to the category of “the historical novel .” The thing he “relished in certain novels was every kind of historical detail.” 7 Lukacs found these details in a variety of novels from across Europe and America. He admired F. Scott Fitzgerald as much as he did Charles Dickens. As early as 1959, Lukacs illustrated to an audience at Bryn Mawr College how these French novelists preserved people, circumstances, and atmospheres from history .10 In that same lectu re he contrasted them with the Russian novelists Leo Tolstoy and Fyodor Dostoyevsky, whom he criticized for their ideological emphases . While Lukacs believed that every novel is histor ical , he also cautioned that some historical novels convey false realities . However, his focus remained on # History. those novelists who formed his own historical thinking . For decades, h e turned to these writers to demonstrate the historicity of the novel. More than any other novelist, Gyula Krúdy molded the way Lukacs thought and wrote . This Hungarian’s novels were one of Lukacs’ great loves, alongside cigars and brandy. He insisted that the novel and history were intertwined art forms, each giving and taking style and content from the other. In Historical Consciousness , Lukacs claimed that “In the broad sense, every novel is a historical novel .” 15 This definition does not adhere to a set of arbitrarily chosen rules. For a novel to be considered historical, it does not need to take place years before the author ’s life . It do es not always recount the political and social events of a time , nor recreate the lives of certain historical personages. Lukacs’s dictum is not an attempt to define the sub -genre. To Lukacs, a ny novel that describe d rea l places, circumstances, and people could be considered historical . He saw the novel as an intrinsically historical genre. Very early in his career, Lukacs went so far as to predict the end of the novel and its absorption into histor ical writing .16 He saw in many twentieth -century novelists an effort to write history with the form of a novel, rather than write a novel with the help of history . The French J ea n Dutourd, American E.L. Doctorow, Russian Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, and many more wrote novels for the primary purpose of preserving history . More forebodingly , in his 1981 essay “Doctorow urlitzer or History in Ragtime ,” Lukacs predict ed the end of serious literature in the West. Despite this later pessimism, Lukacs allowed the novel to greatly influence his writing and teaching styles . Lukacs typically referred to novels from the nineteenth century, which he dubbed, “the golden age of the novel ,” to show the historicity of the genre .18 He was not the first historian to describe novels this way . Forty -six years before the publication of Lukacs’s Historical Consciousness, the English historian Herbert Butterfield indicate the details a historian could find in the novel . He even anticipated Lukacs’s recognition that “ The functions of historians and novelists overlap; their dependence is mutual ; their approach is much the same – description, in prose, always the description of some kind of past .” 19 In his essay The Historical Novel (1924) , Butterfield specifi ed what kind of material the novelist preserves : though we may not seek to gather our historical facts from the novel, there are more subtle things, unconscious prejudices and unformulated sentiments that we take in unawares, there are pictures that haunt us, there is an atmosphere that compels us, and i f we find nothing else we find the sentiment of history, the feeling for the past, in the historical novel. On one side, therefore, the historical novel is a “form” of history. It is a way of treating the past. 20 Butterfield’s distinction between facts and subtle sentiments deserves emphasis. Both he and Lukacs understood that the historian did more than connect a sequence of events or record data. # History. Bourgeois 32 Bibliographical Essay This thesis began as an inquiry into José Ortega y Gasset’s Meditations on Quixote. I intended to study Ortega’s view of the novel and how it influenced John Lukacs. As the project evolved, the focus shifted to Lukacs. However, Ortega remained an instrumental figure to the project insofar as he influenced Lukacs . However, Lukacs became the main study of the project very early. The historiography of Luka cs ’s work is currently sparse. His students (John Rossi and John Rodden) have written multiple articles about him. 88 Other Historians, such as Richard Gamble, Lee Congdon, and John H. Among others, t he historian and diplomat Géza Jeszens ky, a friend of Lukacs, crafted an essay in memory of him. Many mention ed his love of novels, but few went further. Lukacs’s reflections on the novel are intrinsically woven into many of his other themes , such as the democratic age, historical consciousness, and others . For some one to fully understand the novel’s significance , he must be acquainted with these themes. In 2025, I worked with the John Lukacs papers at Notre Dame. Until 2019, no scholar had access to these papers. Even now, only a small group has worked with them. Gamble is the only historian who has both written about Lukacs and studied his archives. Letters to and from novelists, lecture notes, and unpublished drafts added greatly to this project.
